notes: Balaguer's Reformist Party (PR) holds ruling slot 0. MD's slot-1 PRSC is the post-1984 merger of PR and the 1961 Revolutionary Social Christian Party; the 1961 Christian-democratic PRSC goes to slot 14, Lora's anti-re-election MIDA (1969) takes slot 1. Coalition slot 13 = State Sugar Council (CEA) technocracy. PRD slot 3, PCD 4, 14 de Junio 5, MPD (Maoist) 19, Wessin's PQD 20, armed forces 22.

0.name: Partido Reformista
0.text:
The Reformist Party is the governing party of President Joaquín Balaguer, founded in 1963–64 among his followers in exile in New York and carried to power in the June 1966 elections held in the shadow of the US-led intervention. On 1 January 1970 it controls the presidency, Congress and the patronage of the state, and is preparing Balaguer's contested bid for re-election in May.

The Reformists offer order, public works and anti-communism after the chaos of 1965. Their base lies in the peasantry, the Trujillo-era bureaucracy, conservative Catholics and business. Close to Washington and backed by the generals, the party relies on state jobs and road and housing projects, and tolerates harsh repression of the left as the price of stability.

1.name: Movimiento de Integración Democrática Antirreeleccionista
1.text:
MIDA was founded in 1969 by Vice President Francisco Augusto Lora, a long-time Balaguer ally who broke with the president over his plan to seek a second consecutive term. On 1 January 1970 it is the main legal challenger to the Reformists and is rallying anti-re-election conservatives for the May presidential race.

Its programme is that of the Reformists without continuismo: private enterprise, good relations with the United States, firm anti-communism and the principle that no president should succeed himself. It draws on dissident Reformist notables, provincial professionals and businessmen uneasy with Balaguer's personal rule, but lacks the state machine and the army's favour.

2.name: Unión Cívica Nacional
2.text:
The National Civic Union grew out of the civic movement that rose against the Trujillo dynasty in 1961 and dominated the Council of State before losing the December 1962 election to Juan Bosch. Under its founder Viriato Fiallo it backed the 1963 coup and has since withered into a minor party of the capital's professional and commercial elite.

The UCN stands for constitutional government, free enterprise, the rule of law and close alignment with the United States. Its voters are lawyers, doctors, merchants and old anti-Trujillo families in Santo Domingo and Santiago. Small in votes but rich in names and newspapers, it can lend respectability to any coalition seeking to contain both Balaguer's continuismo and the left.

3.name: Partido Revolucionario Dominicano
3.text:
The Dominican Revolutionary Party was founded in exile in Havana in 1939 and won the 1962 election that made Juan Bosch president, only to see him toppled by the military in 1963. After the defeat of the 1965 Constitutionalist uprising and the 1966 election, Bosch left for Europe; secretary-general José Francisco Peña Gómez leads the party at home.

The PRD stands for agrarian reform, labour rights, civil liberties and an end to military tutelage, and refuses to legitimize Balaguer's re-election. Its base is the urban poor of Santo Domingo, workers, teachers and the youth. Harassed and its activists murdered, it remains the largest opposition force, torn between Bosch's radical theses and Peña Gómez's democratic pragmatism.

4.name: Partido Comunista Dominicano
4.text:
The Dominican Communist Party descends from the Popular Socialist Party founded under Trujillo in the 1940s and took its present name in 1965. Banned and working underground, it is led by a younger generation with Narciso Isa Conde among its leading figures, while many of its cadres sit in prison or in exile.

The PCD follows the Soviet line: a national-democratic, anti-imperialist revolution built through mass work among workers, students and slum dwellers, rejecting both Maoist adventurism and guerrilla foquismo. It denounces the 1965 US intervention and Balaguer as Washington's proconsul. Its leverage lies in the university, the teachers' and student federations, some unions and its ties to Moscow and Havana.

5.name: Movimiento Revolucionario 14 de Junio
5.text:
The 14th of June Movement takes its name from the failed Cuban-backed landing against Trujillo in June 1959 and was organized by Manuel Aurelio Tavárez Justo, who died leading a guerrilla rising after the 1963 coup. Its militants fought in the Constitutionalist ranks in 1965; since then the movement has splintered into rival factions and survives largely underground.

The 1J4 holds that only armed revolution can end oligarchic and US domination, and looks to Cuba and the guerrilla foco for inspiration. Its strength lies among students of the Autonomous University of Santo Domingo, young professionals and veterans of the 1965 commandos. Decimated by arrests and killings, it remains a recruiting ground for any new guerrilla venture.

6.name: La Trinitaria Nacionalista
6.text:
The Nationalist Trinitarians are a loose circle of Catholic traditionalists, Hispanist intellectuals and retired officers who invoke Juan Pablo Duarte's secret society of 1838 against what they see as a second American occupation. The landing of US Marines in April 1965 and the Inter-American Peace Force left them bitterly hostile to Washington, though no less hostile to Marxism.

They demand an end to foreign tutelage, a Spanish-Catholic national identity, a closed Haitian border and an authoritarian corporate state free of American advisers. Their audience lies in parishes, the Duartian patriotic societies and nationalist sections of the officer corps. They lack a mass following, but their rhetoric resonates with all who felt humiliated in 1965.

7.name: Departamento Nacional de Investigaciones
7.text:
The National Department of Investigations is the state intelligence service created in 1962 to replace Trujillo's dreaded Military Intelligence Service. Under Balaguer it works alongside the National Police and army intelligence in tracking the PRD, the communists and the guerrilla remnants, and many of its agents served the old regime.

As a power bloc the security apparatus stands for permanent emergency: surveillance, preventive arrests, informers in every barrio and a free hand against so-called terrorists. It answers to the palace rather than to Congress or the courts, and its officers jealously guard their autonomy, even from American advisers. Its leverage lies in its files, its gunmen and its role as the regime's shield in an election year.

8.name: Círculo Musa Sadr
8.text:
The Musa Sadr Circle is a handful of Lebanese Shia families and traders in Santo Domingo and San Pedro de Macorís, part of the wider Levantine migration to the Caribbean, who follow news from Tyre and the activism of Imam Musa al-Sadr. In 1969 al-Sadr became head of Lebanon's new Supreme Islamic Shia Council, and his sermons circulate among them.

The circle is pious, commercial and aloof from Dominican party politics, seeking community dignity, mutual aid and recognition alongside the far larger Christian Arab colony. It favours social justice for the deprived and dialogue with Christians. Its weight lies in shops and import houses, not in votes.

9.name: Discípulos de Nayaf
9.text:
The Disciples of Najaf are a few young Shia émigrés and students who correspond with relatives in southern Lebanon and Iraq and read pamphlets attributed to Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled by the Shah and teaching in Najaf since 1965. In the Dominican Republic they are invisible, meeting in private homes in the capital.

They reject the quietism of their elders and argue that militant clergy must lead Muslims against tyranny, Zionism and American power, which they also see behind the 1965 occupation. Without a mosque, cleric or institution, their leverage is nil, but they form a node through which revolutionary Shia literature reaches the Caribbean.

10.name: Casa de la Daawa
10.text:
The House of the Call is a small prayer circle of Palestinian and Syrian Sunni merchants and a few Dominican converts in Santo Domingo, kept alive by literature and occasional visitors from the Muslim World League, founded in Mecca in 1962 to spread Saudi-backed Islam abroad. There is no mosque in the country; prayers are held in a rented room.

The circle is quietist and loyal to the authorities, preaching strict monotheism, personal piety and obedience to rulers. It welcomes King Faisal's pan-Islamic diplomacy and is fiercely anti-communist, which leaves it entirely at ease with Balaguer. Its influence rests on commercial contacts and Saudi scholarships for promising young converts.

11.name: Célula del Califato
11.text:
The Caliphate Cell is a tiny group of Arab students and young converts who first encountered Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953, while studying in Europe and the Middle East. In Santo Domingo they meet discreetly and translate its tracts into Spanish.

They reject nationalism, parliaments and both superpowers, and preach the restoration of a single caliphate uniting all Muslims, to be won by persuading the holders of power rather than through elections. Their milieu is the university and the youth of the Levantine colony. Without numbers or money, their only asset is ideological intensity.

12.name: Hermanos de la Umma
12.text:
The Brothers of the Ummah are a study circle of sons of Palestinian and Syrian émigrés and a few Dominican students who read Hasan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb, executed in Egypt in 1966. Inspired by the Muslim Brotherhood's network of exiles in Europe, they gather for lessons and charity work in the capital.

They call for a gradual Islamic revival through education, mutual aid and moral reform, oppose atheist communism and Zionism, and distrust American power after 1965. Socially conservative but open to elections, they seek respect for Islam among Dominicans. Their influence is limited to a few families, merchants and students.

13.name: Consejo Estatal del Azúcar
13.text:
The State Sugar Council was created in 1966 to run the sugar mills and vast estates confiscated from the Trujillo family, making the state the country's largest employer and exporter. Its administrators, engineers and political appointees form the backbone of Balaguer's developmental state alongside the planning office and the public works ministry.

As a bloc, the state managers favour authoritarian technocracy without ideological commitment: protected sugar quotas in the US market, public investment, controlled unions and jobs distributed through the palace. Their loyalty is to the president personally rather than to any party. Their leverage lies in payrolls covering tens of thousands of cane workers and in the export revenue that funds the regime.

14.name: Partido Revolucionario Social Cristiano
14.text:
The Revolutionary Social Christian Party was founded in 1961, as the Trujillo regime collapsed, by Catholic activists inspired by the Christian Democratic parties of Venezuela and Chile. A small party that contested the 1962 and 1966 elections, it now stands in the opposition, wary of both Balaguer's continuismo and the PRD.

The PRSC preaches the social doctrine of the Church: agrarian reform, cooperatives, Christian trade unionism and a communitarian third way between capitalism and Marxism, at a distance from both blocs. Its base is the Christian labour confederation CASC, Catholic youth and parish activists. Its leverage lies in the Church's social networks and its links to Venezuela's COPEI and the Christian Democrat International.

15.name: Consejo Nacional de Hombres de Empresa
15.native_full: Consejo Nacional de Hombres de Empresa
15.text:
The National Council of Businessmen was founded in 1963 as the voice of the country's large private firms, from the import-export houses and banks of Santo Domingo to the tobacco and rum families of Santiago. Alongside it stand the private sugar interests, above all Gulf and Western, which bought the Central Romana estate in 1967.

The business elite backs Balaguer's order, tax incentives for industry, cheap labour and close ties with American capital, and fears the PRD's agrarian and labour programme. It lends to the government, finances newspapers and campaigns, and counts friends among the generals. Its leverage lies in credit, investment and the threat of capital flight.

16.name: Librecambistas del Cibao
16.text:
The Free-Traders of the Cibao are a circle of Santiago exporters, tobacco and cacao dealers and young economists trained in the United States who resent the capital's protected industries and the swollen state sector inherited from Trujillo. They gather around the Santiago business associations and the Catholic University Madre y Maestra, founded there in 1962.

They call for selling off state enterprises, lower tariffs, sound money, open export markets and a smaller bureaucracy, and look to Puerto Rico's Operation Bootstrap as a model. Pro-American and anti-communist, they distrust Balaguer's patronage economy. Their leverage lies in export earnings, regional pride and the press of Santiago.

17.name: Guardianes de la Cordillera
17.text:
The Guardians of the Cordillera are foresters, botanists, teachers and mountain farmers alarmed at the clearing of the Cordillera Central, whose pine forests feed the rivers of the Cibao. Their cause won a hearing in 1967 when Balaguer ordered the sawmills closed and logging banned, enforced by the armed forces.

They campaign for national parks, reforestation, protection of watersheds such as the Yaque del Norte and an end to slash-and-burn clearing, while many peasants accuse them of serving landlords and soldiers. Politically neutral, they rely on scientific prestige, Catholic ideas of stewardship and the president's own interest in the forests.

18.name: Los Constitucionalistas
18.text:
The Constitutionalists are the veterans of the April 1965 uprising that sought to restore Juan Bosch's constitution of 1963: rebel officers, commandos and civilians who fought the San Isidro generals and the US intervention. Their hero, Colonel Francisco Caamaño Deñó, was posted abroad as military attaché in London and vanished in 1967; rumours place him in Cuba.

They stand for national sovereignty, the 1963 constitution, land reform and a people's army, sitting between the PRD's democratic left and the Marxist parties without joining any bloc. Purged officers, barrio commanders and students sustain the cause. Their leverage is moral authority and the threat of an armed return.

19.name: Movimiento Popular Dominicano
19.text:
The Dominican Popular Movement was founded by exiles in Havana in 1956, returned home in 1960 and became the country's main Maoist organization after the Sino-Soviet split. Banned and hunted, it wages urban armed actions, and its cadres, including its leader Maximiliano Gómez, have faced arrest, torture and assassination.

The MPD calls for a people's war against Balaguer, the landlords and American imperialism, and rejects the Soviet-aligned Communist Party as revisionist. It draws on students, the slum youth of Santo Domingo and some peasant zones. Its leverage lies in clandestine cells, daring armed actions and the radicalized university.

20.name: Partido Quisqueyano Demócrata
20.text:
The Quisqueyan Democratic Party was founded in 1968 around General Elías Wessin y Wessin, the San Isidro commander who led the loyalist forces against the Constitutionalists in 1965 and was then removed under US pressure. It is preparing to contest the 1970 elections with Wessin as its standard-bearer.

The PQD offers hard anti-communism, law and order, the honour of the armed forces and a nationalist appeal to forgotten Dominicans, attacking both Balaguer's cronies and the left. Its base is retired and serving officers, Catholic conservatives, police families and lower-middle-class voters frightened by 1965. Its leverage lies in sympathies within the barracks.

21.name: Los Calieses
21.text:
The Calieses take their name from the informers of Trujillo's Military Intelligence Service and denote the dispersed network of former agents, militiamen and party bosses of the dictatorship who survived its fall in 1961. The dynasty's heir, Ramfis Trujillo, died in exile in Madrid in December 1969, leaving the family's fortune and followers abroad.

They yearn for the Era of Trujillo: one leader, one party, total surveillance, the cult of the Benefactor, anti-Haitian racial nationalism and the annihilation of communists. Many have found shelter in Balaguer's police and bureaucracy. Their leverage lies in old files, contacts in the security services and men accustomed to violence.

22.name: Fuerzas Armadas de la República Dominicana
22.english: Armed Forces of the Dominican Republic
22.native_full: Fuerzas Armadas de la República Dominicana
22.text:
The Armed Forces of the Dominican Republic, built up by Trujillo into one of the largest militaries in the Caribbean, remain the arbiter of national politics after toppling Bosch in 1963 and fighting the Constitutionalists in 1965. Balaguer has purged the rebels, rotated commanders and courted rival generals such as Neit Nivar Seijas and Enrique Pérez y Pérez.

The officer corps is anti-communist, US-trained and equipped, and jealous of its privileges, from smuggling and land to political appointments. The San Isidro air base remains the symbol of its power. Rival cliques compete for the president's favour, and the military's support is the true foundation of the regime.
22.wiki: Armed Forces of the Dominican Republic

23.name: Hispanistas de la Corona
23.text:
The Hispanists of the Crown are a small circle of Catholic intellectuals, landed families and admirers of Franco's Spain who cultivate the memory of Spanish rule, from the colonial capital of Santo Domingo to the brief re-annexation to Spain in 1861–1865. They welcomed Franco's designation of Prince Juan Carlos as his royal successor in July 1969.

They celebrate Hispanidad, the Catholic faith and hierarchy as the essence of Dominican identity, opposing both American mass culture and Afro-Caribbean influences from Haiti. Their politics is cultural rather than partisan, but they move in the academies, the old Santo Domingo families and the diplomatic world of Madrid.
